transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I suppose what brings me in is… I just can’t seem to sit still much anymore. Or maybe it’s not “anymore,” but it’s gotten more noticeable this past year or so. I’m always puttering around the house, fixing little things, rearranging drawers, signing up to help with one more thing when I probably should just sit down.

Even at 87, you’d think I’d be happy to rest, but I get antsy just sitting there. My daughter says, “Mother, just relax,” and I’ll say I am relaxing, but then I’m up straightening the magazines or checking the kitchen. It’s not anything dramatic, I guess, but it feels like I’m always in motion.
Does this constant need to be in motion cause you any distress?

Yes, it does, a bit. I mean, I try not to make a fuss about it, but I do feel badly afterward sometimes. At the senior center, for instance—oh, they have this little sign-up table, and everyone gets in a muddle about who’s bringing cookies and who’s driving whom, and I suppose I can get a little… brisk.

I’ve had to apologize after meetings because I could tell I’d made people tense. One friend even suggested maybe I take a smaller role at the table, which stung a little, honestly. I don’t mean to upset anyone. I just get going and then it’s hard to soften myself down.
Do you find yourself having repetitive thoughts that you feel compelled to act on when you're puttering around or fixing things?

Repetitive thoughts… hmm. I’m not sure I’d put it that way. It’s more that I notice something and then I’m up doing it before I’ve really decided to. Like, if a picture is crooked or the tea towels are in the wrong drawer—well, “wrong” according to me, I suppose—I just go fix it.

But I don’t know that there’s a particular thought I’m having over and over, or that I feel I must do it or something terrible will happen. It’s more… I see it, I move. Then while I’m doing that, I remember the plant needs water, and then I’m in the kitchen, and—oh, I had a neighbor once who used to label every single shelf in her pantry, very tidy woman, but that’s not really me. I just get going.
Do you feel like something bad would happen if you didn't fix those things, like the picture or the tea towels?

No, I don’t think so. Not “something bad,” exactly. It’s not like I’m afraid the house will fall down because a picture is crooked.

It’s more that I see it and my hand is already reaching, if that makes sense. Like when my mother used to straighten the lace doilies—oh, she had doilies on everything, even the arms of the chairs, drove my father mad—but for me it’s just… I notice it, and then I’m fixing it before I’ve quite thought it through.
Do you feel like things need to be done perfectly, or just that they need to be done?

Not perfectly, no… I wouldn’t say that. It’s not like I’m polishing the silver until I can see my face in it—though my aunt used to do that before company came, every Sunday practically.

For me it’s more that things need doing, and once I notice them I’m already up. That’s really part of why I came in, I suppose. This past year or so I feel like I’m always puttering—fixing this, arranging that, saying yes to one more little job or volunteer thing—and even at 87 I can’t seem to just sit down and be still for very long.
Do you feel like your puttering and fixing things helps you feel more in control of your environment?

Maybe a little, but I don’t think of it as “control,” really. It’s more… if I’m up and doing something, I feel better than just sitting there noticing everything.

What brings me in is that for the past year or so, I seem to be constantly puttering—fixing this, arranging that, signing myself up to help with one more thing. I’ll tell myself I’m just going to sit with my tea, and then I notice a plant, or a drawer, or remember someone at church needed a call—well, not always church, sometimes the library group—and off I go.

At 87, you’d think I’d be better at sitting still, wouldn’t you? But I have a hard time just being still.
Do you feel like your puttering and fixing things is making your environment more orderly?

I suppose it does make things a bit neater, yes, but I don’t think that’s really the main thing. I mean, if the tea towels are folded straight, well, that’s nice, isn’t it? My grandmother could fold linens so crisply you’d think they came from a hotel, and she never wasted a motion.

But for me lately—this past year or so—it’s more that I’m just always up doing something. Puttering, fixing a little thing here, arranging something there, agreeing to help with one more volunteer bit. And then I look up and realize I never actually sat down with my tea like I meant to.

So maybe the house ends up more orderly, but I think the bigger thing is I have a hard time being still, even at 87.
Do you find that you're particularly bothered by things being asymmetrical or not exactly as they should be?

Asymmetrical… not especially, I don’t think. I mean, if a picture is hanging crooked I might straighten it, but I don’t sit there feeling upset because it’s not exactly so.

My sister-in-law used to be very particular about things lining up on the mantel—little porcelain birds, all facing the same way—and I remember thinking, goodness, that seems like a lot to keep track of. I’m not like that, no. If something catches my eye, I may fix it, but I wouldn’t say I’m particularly bothered by it being uneven or not perfect.
Do you feel like you're doing these activities because they help keep your mind engaged?

I suppose it does keep my mind busy, yes, though I don’t always think of it that way. It’s more like I notice one little thing and then another, and before I know it I’ve fixed the shelf, rearranged the papers, called someone about volunteering—oh, and then the kettle’s gone cold.

This past year or so, that’s been the pattern. I’m always puttering or arranging or signing myself up for one more thing. Even at 87, I seem to have a hard time just sitting down and being still.
Do you think you're doing all these activities to avoid thinking about something else?

I don’t think so, no—not avoiding something in particular. I mean, I have the usual thoughts anyone has at my age, I suppose, but it’s not as if I’m trying not to think about one certain thing.

It’s more that I’m just always moving from one little task to the next. I’ll putter in the kitchen, then fix something that’s been crooked, then arrange a drawer, then say yes to another volunteer thing before I’ve even thought it through. My neighbor used to say, “Sit down before you wear a path in the floor,” and lately I think she’d be right.

So no, I wouldn’t say it’s avoidance exactly. What brings me in is more that for the past year or so, I can’t seem to just sit still, even at 87.
Do you feel like you're doing these activities mainly because they help keep your mind active?

Maybe partly, but I wouldn’t say “mainly” in a deliberate way. It’s not as if I wake up and think, I must keep my mind active today.

It’s more that I just seem to keep going—puttering around, fixing little things, arranging this or that, and then someone asks about a volunteer job and I say yes before I’ve really sat with it. My mother was like that too, always had a dish towel in her hand, though she at least seemed to finish one thing before starting another.

But yes, what brings me in is that for the past year or so, I’ve had such a hard time just sitting down and being still, even at 87.
Do you think you would feel bored or unfulfilled if you weren't constantly doing these activities?

I suppose I might feel a bit restless, more than bored exactly. “Unfulfilled” sounds a little grand for it, doesn’t it? I’m not climbing mountains—I’m straightening the pantry or fixing a loose handle or saying yes to help with some little volunteer thing.

But yes, if I’m not doing something, I do seem to get up and find something to do. I’ll sit down with tea, and then notice the cushions are crooked, and then I’m in the other room sorting something. My niece says I’m like one of those wind-up toys—she had one as a child, a little tin chicken, I think.

What brings me in is that for the past year or so I just feel like I’m always puttering, fixing, arranging, or taking on one more thing, and even at 87 I have a hard time simply sitting still.
Do you feel like you're doing these activities because you would otherwise feel mentally unstimulated?

I don’t know that I’d put it as “mentally unstimulated,” exactly. That sounds like I’m doing a crossword to keep the brain sharp—my sister used to do those in ink, which always seemed very confident to me.

For me it’s more… I just don’t seem to stop. What brings me in is that for the past year or so I feel like I’m always puttering, fixing something, arranging things, or volunteering for one more thing, and even at 87 I have a hard time just sitting down and being still. So maybe it’s stimulation in a way, but it doesn’t feel like I’m choosing it for that reason.
Do you feel like you need to be physically active to feel comfortable?

Yes, I think so—comfortable is a good word for it, actually. If I sit too long, I start noticing things that need doing. A drawer that doesn’t close quite right, a plant that needs turning toward the window, someone from the church asking for help with a sign-up sheet—oh, I used to be very good with those, though now everyone wants things online, which is a nuisance.

But yes, for the past year or so I just feel like I’m always up and doing something—puttering, fixing, arranging, or saying yes to one more thing. Even at 87, I have a hard time just sitting down and being still.
Do you feel like you need to be active in order to keep your mind from wandering or feeling empty?

Maybe, though I don’t know that it feels like my mind would be “empty.” It’s more that if I stop, I don’t stay stopped. I sit down and then I’m up again, fussing with something—straightening, fixing, arranging. Just yesterday I was going to rest and somehow ended up reorganizing a little shelf, which I’m sure did not need reorganizing.

What brings me in is really that for the past year or so, I feel like I’m always puttering or taking on one more thing, like volunteering to help here or there, and even at 87 I have a hard time just sitting down and being still.
Do you feel like your actions are driven by a desire to make things perfect?

Perfect? No, I don’t think that’s quite it. I mean, I like things decent, you know—my mother used to say a room should look “ready for company,” though heaven knows company doesn’t announce itself much anymore.

But I don’t know that I’m trying to make things perfect. Sometimes I just notice something and then I’m doing it before I’ve really decided to. A crooked stack of papers, a little thing out of place… but not because it has to be flawless, exactly. It’s more just… I don’t leave it alone.
Do you feel like your actions are helping you maintain a sense of control over your daily life?

Control… maybe a little, but I don’t really think of it that way. It’s more that I’m just always doing something before I’ve quite planned to—puttering around, fixing this, arranging that, saying yes when someone needs help with one more thing.

And I suppose keeping busy does make the day feel… structured, maybe? Though at my age you’d think I’d have earned the right to sit quietly. But for the past year or so, I just haven’t been very good at that. Even when I mean to rest, I’m up again doing something.
Do you feel less anxious when you're puttering or fixing things?

Less anxious… I’m not sure I’d say that, exactly. I haven’t really kept track of it that way. Sometimes I’m just already up and doing something before I’ve had a chance to ask myself how I feel.

I suppose there’s a little comfort in having my hands busy, but whether that’s anxiety or just habit—well, I don’t know. My sister used to crochet whenever she sat down, and she’d make these long, lopsided scarves for everyone, even people who didn’t need scarves. I’m not crocheting, of course, I’m usually just moving things around.

So… I can’t say for sure that I feel less anxious. It’s more that I notice I’m doing it, and then I’m already halfway through it.
Do you feel like puttering or fixing things helps calm you down?

Calm me down… maybe, though I don’t know that I’d put it quite that way. It’s more that I can’t seem to stop myself from doing it. For the past year or so, I’m always puttering around—fixing something, straightening things, arranging this or that, or volunteering when somebody needs “just one little favor,” which never is little, of course.

Even at 87, you’d think I’d be better at sitting still. My neighbor can sit with her tea for ages and watch the birds like it’s a full-time job. I try that, and then I notice a drawer needs closing or a plant needs turning, and up I go. So maybe it settles me a bit, but mostly it’s just… I have a hard time being still.
Do you feel like you have to do these things, or is it just something you want to do?

I don’t know that I want to, exactly. It feels more like… I’m already doing it before I’ve decided. Like I’ll mean to sit down, and then I see something that needs fixing or straightening, or someone asks for one more little favor and I’m saying yes.

For the past year or so, that’s really what brought me in—I’m always puttering, arranging things, volunteering for something, and even at 87 I can’t seem to just sit still very well. My cousin used to say “idle hands are the devil’s workshop,” though she mostly used that to make us wash dishes after supper. But yes… it feels less like a choice sometimes, and more like I just have to keep moving.

But yes, for the past year or so I just feel like I’m always up and doing something—puttering, fixing, arranging, or saying yes to one more thing. Even at 87, I have a hard time just sitting down and being still.

Maybe, though I don’t know that it feels like my mind would be “empty.” It’s more that if I stop, I don’t stay stopped. I sit down and then I’m up again, fussing with something—straightening, fixing, arranging. Just yesterday I was going to rest and somehow ended up reorganizing a little shelf, which I’m sure did not need reorganizing.

What brings me in is really that for the past year or so, I feel like I’m always puttering or taking on one more thing, like volunteering to help here or there, and even at 87 I have a hard time just sitting down and being still.

patient.answer:
Perfect? No, I don’t think that’s quite it. I mean, I like things decent, you know—my mother used to say a room should look “ready for company,” though heaven knows company doesn’t announce itself much anymore.

But I don’t know that I’m trying to make things perfect. Sometimes I just notice something and then I’m doing it before I’ve really decided to. A crooked stack of papers, a little thing out of place… but not because it has to be flawless, exactly. It’s more just… I don’t leave it alone.

Control… maybe a little, but I don’t really think of it that way. It’s more that I’m just always doing something before I’ve quite planned to—puttering around, fixing this, arranging that, saying yes when someone needs help with one more thing.

And I suppose keeping busy does make the day feel… structured, maybe? Though at my age you’d think I’d have earned the right to sit quietly. But for the past year or so, I just haven’t been very good at that. Even when I mean to rest, I’m up again doing something.

doctor.question: Do you feel less anxious when you're puttering or fixing things?

patient.answer:
Less anxious… I’m not sure I’d say that, exactly. I haven’t really kept track of it that way. Sometimes I’m just already up and doing something before I’ve had a chance to ask myself how I feel.

I suppose there’s a little comfort in having my hands busy, but whether that’s anxiety or just habit—well, I don’t know. My sister used to crochet whenever she sat down, and she’d make these long, lopsided scarves for everyone, even people who didn’t need scarves. I’m not crocheting, of course, I’m usually just moving things around.

So… I can’t say for sure that I feel less anxious. It’s more that I notice I’m doing it, and then I’m already halfway through it.

patient.answer:
Calm me down… maybe, though I don’t know that I’d put it quite that way. It’s more that I can’t seem to stop myself from doing it. For the past year or so, I’m always puttering around—fixing something, straightening things, arranging this or that, or volunteering when somebody needs “just one little favor,” which never is little, of course.

Even at 87, you’d think I’d be better at sitting still. My neighbor can sit with her tea for ages and watch the birds like it’s a full-time job. I try that, and then I notice a drawer needs closing or a plant needs turning, and up I go. So maybe it settles me a bit, but mostly it’s just… I have a hard time being still.

I don’t know that I want to, exactly. It feels more like… I’m already doing it before I’ve decided. Like I’ll mean to sit down, and then I see something that needs fixing or straightening, or someone asks for one more little favor and I’m saying yes.

For the past year or so, that’s really what brought me in—I’m always puttering, arranging things, volunteering for something, and even at 87 I can’t seem to just sit still very well. My cousin used to say “idle hands are the devil’s workshop,” though she mostly used that to make us wash dishes after supper. But yes… it feels less like a choice sometimes, and more like I just have to keep moving.
